description: Painted by **Leonardo da Vinci** between **1503** and **1519**, the *Mona Lisa* became the absolute icon of the Louvre. Technique, a mysterious smile, and a theft in **1911** that changed everything.

hero.hook: A smile, a theft, a myth: how one portrait became the most famous work in the world.

blocks.text: The *Mona Lisa*, painted between **1503** and **1519** by **Leonardo da Vinci**, is the most visited painting in the world. On show at the **Louvre**, it fascinates as much for its technique as for its story. It is not only a fine portrait. It is a myth built by art, by science and by a news story.
Why this face rather than another? Because Leonardo packed his innovations into it, and because a spectacular theft made it famous across the planet.

The portrait was begun in Florence around **1503**. The man who ordered it was the merchant **Francesco del Giocondo**. The model was most likely his wife, [[Lisa Gherardini]]. But Leonardo never delivered the painting. He kept it, reworked it for years, and carried it to France, where he died in **1519**.

blocks.caption: The Mona Lisa at the Louvre: a small poplar panel turned world icon

blocks.text: His signature technique is [[Leonardian sfumato]]: glazes, extremely thin layers, that erase the outlines. No hard line is left. The face melts into the air. Leonardo also uses [[Aerial perspective]]: the distant landscape turns bluer and softer, exactly as it does in real sight.

The famous smile is not only a painted emotion. It plays with our [[Peripheral vision]]. When you stare at the model's eyes, the edge of the retina reads the mouth as soft shadow, and the smile seems to be there. Look straight at the mouth and it fades.

blocks.caption: The harder you stare, the more the smile slips away

blocks.text: Leonardo, painter and scientist at once, studied optics. Part of the mystery of the smile rests on exact knowledge of how the human eye handles shadow.
The result: the face looks alive, shifting, almost aware of being watched.

sections.title: The smile that plays with the eye

blocks.text: In the 19th century, the *Mona Lisa* was admired, but not yet the top work of the Louvre. Everything changed on **August 21, 1911**. [[Vincenzo Peruggia]], an Italian glazier at the museum, took it down: this was [[The theft of the Mona Lisa (1911)]]. He hid it under his smock and walked calmly out.

blocks.caption: 1911: the empty wall makes headlines and creates a star

blocks.text: The investigation turned into a scandal. The poet [[Guillaume Apollinaire]] spent a week in jail. [[Pablo Picasso]] was questioned. When the painting reappeared in **1913**, it was no longer only a painting. It was a celebrity.

Today the little poplar panel lives behind [[Bulletproof glass]], inside a climate-controlled case. Acid attacks, objects thrown at it: the protection became necessary. And the parodies, from Duchamp to the internet, prove that the painting has become a universal language.

blocks.text: The *Mona Lisa* owes its fame as much to Leonardo's genius (sfumato, the optical smile) as to history: a theft in 1911 turned an admired masterpiece into a global icon.
